1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: The mechanism matches the expert exactly: a hard-coded session+probe table transcribed from the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m (rather than globbing), h5py for the v7.3 data structures, scipy.io for motionEnergy_*.mat, and correct exclusion of the two *_BilatMC_Behavior folders (the AI verified they contain no 'clu' field). The 25 fixed-delay entries and their probe assignments are identical to the expert's, including the two-probe JEB15 sessions. The concern is scope: DATA_DIR is hard-wired to /app/data/Ephys_Behavior, so the 19 randomized-delay sessions in RandomizedDelay_Ephys_Behavior -- which are listed in the authors' own loadJEB11/12/23/24_ALMVideo.m, are part of the paper's ALM dataset (845 units, 4 mice), and are shipped in /app/data -- are never loaded. That is 43% of the expert's sessions, 4 of 14 mice, 6,336 of 13,762 trials. The stated reasons (a separate task variant whose sample/delay epochs land at variable times, and almost no WC trials) are coherent and the second is factually right (those sessions contribute only ~87 WC trials), but the go-cue alignment, the decoder inputs and all six outputs are well-defined for randomized-delay sessions, so nothing in the task actually forces their exclusion. A defensible scoping choice that a human should sign off on, not an error. The AI also never implements a scipy.io fallback for data_structure files, which would have been required for the 11 v5-format randomized-delay files -- an implementation constraint that is not mentioned as a reason.
1-a.code_correctness_justification: The code loads exactly the 25 sessions it lists, with the probes it lists, using h5py for data structures and scipy.io for motion energy, and it reports 25 sessions / 10 subjects / 1531 units / 7426 trials, consistent with the described scope.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same rule as the expert: the animal id is the part of the session name before the date (here the first element of the hard-coded tuple), and subject_idx indexes into a list of unique animals aligned with the session order. The only difference is ordering -- the expert sorts the animal set, the AI keeps first-appearance order -- which is immaterial since subject_idx is built consistently with the same list. 10 subjects instead of 14 is a consequence of the session-scope decision in 1-a, not of a different subject-splitting rule.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: subjects is appended on first sight of each animal and subject_idx = subjects.index(anm) is appended in the same loop that appends the session's neural/input/output, so the arrays stay aligned; the verifier reports 10 subjects with the correct per-subject session counts (JEB13:5, JEB14:4, JEB15:4, JEB19:4, JEB7:2, JGR2:2, rest 1).

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: The per-session logic matches the expert: one data_structure file = one session = one element of neural/input/output, two-probe sessions concatenated into a single population rather than split, and the fixed-delay/randomized-delay distinction is not used to create separate datasets. The AI adds a session-level QC the expert does not have -- drop sessions with <10 units (the paper's own inclusion criterion) or <2 trials -- which is well justified and in practice a no-op. The rating is driven by the same issue as 1-a: only the 25 fixed-delay sessions become sessions in the output, so the delivered dataset is 25 rather than 44 sessions.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: process_session returns one set of per-trial lists per file, main() appends one entry per session to each top-level list, and the MIN_UNITS / <2-trial guards are implemented as described (and printed nothing, i.e. dropped nothing).

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: trials are the rows of the Bpod table obj.bp, with Ntrials as the count and one goCue per trial; spikes carry their own 1-based trial number and each camera trial has its own frameTimes/ts cell, so no trial boundary is reconstructed. Unlike the expert, the AI does not truncate bp fields to Ntrials, but it verified beforehand (trajectory step 77) that every relevant field has exactly Ntrials entries in all 25 sessions it uses, that goCue has no NaNs, and that R+L==1 and hit+miss+no==1 on every trial, so the truncation is unnecessary within its scope.
1-d.code_correctness_justification: load_behavior reads Ntrials and every per-trial flag as flat vectors of that length; spike trial indices are converted with -1 and used to index align_times; trial_pos maps original trial numbers to kept-trial rows. Per-session trial counts match the expert's exactly on all 25 shared sessions.

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert's two documented filters: drop early-lick (bp.early) and photostimulation (bp.stim.enable) trials, following every params.condition in the paper's scripts, and deliberately keep ignore/no-response trials so that 'none'/'ignore' output classes exist. The expert has a third filter for trials that fall after the end of the ephys recording; I verified independently that on all 25 fixed-delay sessions the maximum spiking trial number equals Ntrials, so that filter is a no-op here -- and indeed the AI's per-session trial counts (252, 390, 302, ...) match the expert's exactly on every shared session. The AI does not drop trials for missing video, same as the expert.
1-e.code_correctness_justification: trial_mask = (~early) & (~stim) is computed once and used for both the spike binning (via trial_pos) and the final assembly loop (over `keep`); session_info reports 661 early and 173 stim trials excluded and 7,426 kept, consistent.

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source as the expert: obj.clu{probe}.quality, .trial and .trialtm for the probe(s) named in the authors' load scripts, with obj.bp.ev.goCue supplying the alignment. Units from both probes of a two-probe session are concatenated into one population, as in the expert solution.
2-a.code_correctness_justification: load_spikes dereferences exactly quality/trial/trialtm per cluster for each probe in `probes` and appends all surviving clusters from all probes into one list, giving a (n_units, n_trials, n_bins) array per session.

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Different implementation of the same reference operation, equally well justified. Both convert spike counts to Hz and smooth along time with the paper's params.smooth = 15 kernel and no normalisation/z-scoring. The expert approximates mySmooth with a symmetric gaussian_filter1d of sigma = 14 ms (the sd of gausswin(15) at 5 ms bins); the AI ports mySmooth literally -- gausswin(15) with alpha=2.5, the first floor(15/2)=7 taps zeroed to make it causal, renormalised, with MATLAB's 'reflect' boundary (which prepends the first N samples and trims them, exactly as the MATLAB does). The causal port is arguably the more faithful reading of the paper ('smooth with causal gaussian kernel'). The trade-off is that with 10 ms bins the same 15-tap kernel spans twice as much time as at the expert's 5 ms bins (sigma ~28 ms causal vs 14 ms symmetric), so the AI's rates are smoothed roughly twice as heavily and are delayed rather than centred. Neither choice is wrong; both are internally consistent with a dt used somewhere in the authors' scripts.
2-b.code_correctness_justification: I checked the port line by line against utils/mySmooth.m: the kernel formula matches MATLAB's gausswin, kern[:n//2]=0 matches kern(1:floor(numel(kern)/2))=0, the prepend-then-trim (padded[n:]) matches out(trim:end) with trim=N+1 under 1-based indexing, and np.convolve(...,'same') with a kernel whose leading half is zero is genuinely causal. Smoothing is applied along the time axis (counts transposed to (NT, n_trials)) and division by DT happens before smoothing, giving Hz.

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Well justified but more permissive than the expert. Both apply findClusters.m's drop list for params.quality={'all'} plus the paper's mean-rate > 1 Hz criterion. The AI uses exactly the four labels in findClusters.m (garbage, gabrga, noisy, real?) and, like the expert, matches them case-insensitively after stripping because the labels are free text; the expert additionally drops 'poor', which is not in the authors' list. As a result the AI keeps substantially more units (1,531 vs the expert's 1,220 on the same 25 sessions; e.g. 48 vs 25 for EKH1, 141 vs 99 for JEB15) -- 'Poor' is a large label category (42 of 141 surviving units in JEB15). Keeping them is literally what the paper's code does, so it is at least as well justified as the expert's extra cut, though it means more marginal units enter the decoder. The AI additionally imposes the paper's >=10 units/session rule, which the expert does not (no session was affected).
2-c.code_correctness_justification: BAD_QUALITY is applied to qual.lower().strip() before any rate is computed, non-string labels become '' via _char and are kept, and the 1 Hz cut is applied to rates.mean(axis=(1,2)) (mean over kept trials and all bins) with a strict '>' as the paper states. qualities is filtered with the same mask so session_info stays aligned.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert and to alignSpikes.m: trialtm is already on the behaviour clock and relative to trial start, so the alignment is the single subtraction trialtm - goCue[trial], with no offset or interpolation. ALIGN_EVENT='goCue' for both DR and WC trials. The AI additionally sanity-checked the alignment empirically (tongue visibility, motion energy and population rate all step up immediately after t=0).
2-d.code_correctness_justification: times = times - align_times[trials] uses the spike's own trial (after the -1 conversion from MATLAB's 1-based numbering), and the [TMIN, TMAX) mask plus floor((t-TMIN)/DT) places each spike in the bin containing it.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: The window (-2.5 to +2.5 s), the uniform grid, and the absence of any rebinning all match the expert; only the bin size differs, 10 ms vs the expert's 5 ms, giving 500 instead of 1000 bins. Both values appear in the authors' code: getDefaultParams.m and Figure1e.m use params.dt = 1/200, while WorkingWithDataObjs.m, EDFigure2a, EDFigure3, dimensionality.m and all behaviour scripts use 1/100. The AI grepped for this and chose 1/100 with the citation in the header, so the choice is sourced rather than arbitrary. It does halve the temporal resolution of the delivered dataset relative to the expert's and changes T in the summary statistics, and it interacts with the bin-indexed smoothing kernel (see 2-b), but it is a legitimate reading of the reference code.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: EDGES/TAXIS reproduce getSeq.m's `edges = tmin:dt:tmax; obj.time = edges + dt/2; obj.time = obj.time(1:end-1)` exactly (500 centres, -2.495..2.495); metadata['time_bin_size'] is 10.0 ms and all trials/sessions have T=500 per the verifier output. Spikes are histogrammed directly onto this grid and the camera streams are interpolated onto the same centres -- nothing is binned finely and then rebinned.

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: the input is not read from the data but defined by the alignment window itself -- go cue at t=0, -2.5 to +2.5 s -- and is the vector of bin centres.
3-a.code_correctness_justification: TAXIS is the module-level bin-centre vector; input_names is ['time_from_go_cue'] and the verifier reports the input range as [-2.495, 2.495].

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: None, same as the expert: the axis is cast to float32, shaped (1, 500), and repeated for every trial of every session. The decoder spec asks for a continuous time-varying input, and both solutions supply the ramp rather than a binary event marker.
3-b.code_correctness_justification: time_input = TAXIS.astype(np.float32).reshape(1, NT) and input_trials.append(time_input.copy()) per kept trial; shape (1, 500) matches d_input=1.

3-c.question: How is the `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same construction as the expert: the input is the centre vector of the very grid the spikes are histogrammed into, so bin k is the same interval in the input and in the neural data, and the camera streams are sampled at the same centres.
3-c.code_correctness_justification: floor((t - TMIN)/DT) for spikes and TAXIS = EDGES[:-1] + DT/2 are the same partition of [-2.5, 2.5]; interp_nan is evaluated at TAXIS for the video streams.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same variables as the expert -- instructed side (R, and here L explicitly rather than as the complement of R) plus the hit/miss outcome flags -- and the same reasoning that the licked side is not recorded and must be inferred. The AI additionally cites the authors' getPrevChoice.m, which derives choice from exactly this combination.
4-a.code_correctness_justification: R, L, hit, miss are all read as per-trial booleans in load_behavior and only these are used in the lick-direction expression.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: Logically identical to the expert: hit means the animal licked the instructed port, miss means it licked the other one, anything else is no lick. Codes are the same (left 0, right 1, none 2) and the per-trial value is broadcast across all time bins, as the expert also does. The AI writes it as two explicit masks ((R&hit)|(L&miss) for right) rather than the expert's np.where on hit/miss, but the mapping is the same on every trial because R and L are exact complements (verified in the trajectory).
4-b.code_correctness_justification: lick_dir defaults to 2, then left and right masks overwrite it; out[0] = lick_dir[trial] broadcasts over the 500 bins; output_values[0] = ['left','right','none'] matches the codes. The resulting fractions (0.402/0.427/0.172) are close to the expert's (0.423/0.446/0.131), the difference being the larger ignore-trial share in fixed-delay sessions.

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Behavioral context* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same single field as the expert, obj.bp.autowater. The AI also checked that autowater trials occur in contiguous blocks (95-98% of adjacent autowater trials are consecutive), confirming the flag marks WC blocks rather than scattered free-water trials.
5-a.code_correctness_justification: beh['autowater'] = _vec(bp,'autowater') > 0.5 is the only input to the context computation.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Behavioral context*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: A direct relabelling with the same codes as the expert and the spec: autowater -> WC (0), everything else -> DR (1), broadcast across bins.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: context = np.where(beh['autowater'], 0, 1); output_values[1] = ['WC','DR']. Observed fractions 0.167 WC / 0.833 DR; the difference from the expert's 0.097/0.903 is entirely attributable to the excluded randomized-delay sessions, which contain almost no WC trials.

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: hit and miss, with ignore inferred as the complement. The AI additionally loads bp.no (and verified hit+miss+no == 1 on every trial of every session) but does not use it in the computation, which is the same logic the expert applies.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: Only beh['hit'] and beh['miss'] index into the outcome array; beh['no'] is read but unused (a harmless leftover, noted under 11-d).

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert: miss -> incorrect (0), hit -> correct (1), everything else -> ignore (2), with the spec's code ordering, broadcast across bins, and ignore trials retained rather than dropped (the paper omits them; both solutions keep them so the other five outputs remain available).
6-b.code_correctness_justification: outcome is initialised to 2 and overwritten by miss then hit; output_values[2] = ['incorrect','correct','ignore']. Observed fractions 0.134/0.694/0.172 are consistent with the lick-direction 'none' fraction (0.172), as they must be.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses obj.traj view 0 (side camera) feature 'tongue' only, plus that view's frameTimes and the sglx bitcode/bp.ev.bitStart fields needed for the clock offset. The expert additionally uses the bottom camera's 'top_tongue' and merges the two views, arguing that the two cameras disagree about which frames show the tongue so using both recovers more of the lick bout. The AI's own measurements support that the two views are comparably sparse (side tongue NaN 0.907, bottom top_tongue NaN 0.912) but it did not check their overlap, and it gave no explicit reason for preferring the side view (its code comment cites params.traj_features, which in fact lists tongue features for both cameras). Using the canonical side view alone is a standard and defensible choice -- it is the view the paper's tongue analyses feature -- and it avoids the cross-view rescaling the expert needed. The cost is visible in the statistics: 92.1% of bins are 'not visible' versus the expert's 87.5%.
7-a.code_correctness_justification: TONGUE_FEATURES = [(0,'tongue')] is the only tongue entry, and view_data/pos are keyed by (view, feature) so exactly that one trace is read and used.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: A different but equally defensible pipeline: the AI ports the authors' findPosition.m/findVelocity.m -- interpolate x and y onto the analysis time axis, do not smooth tongue features (the MATLAB explicitly skips smoothing for tongue), do not subtract baseline drift (also tongue-specific in the MATLAB), then take the gradient within each contiguous visible run and the magnitude of the two components. The expert instead computes the velocity at native frame resolution after a 5 ms gaussian and then averages into bins. The AI's approach follows the reference code more literally; the expert's preserves more of the 400 Hz signal, since sampling the interpolated position at 100 Hz can miss short protrusions and aliases the fast tongue kinematics. Both correctly deviate from the MATLAB in one respect required by the spec: where the MATLAB zeroes the tongue velocity when the tongue is not visible, both keep it missing so it can become the 'not visible' class. No cross-view normalisation is needed here because only one view is used.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: speed_from_position(..., fill=False) leaves NaNs unfilled, splits the visible indices on gaps (np.diff(idx) > 1), applies np.gradient per run, assigns 0 to singleton runs, and returns hypot(vx,vy) together with the pre-fill visibility mask; interp_nan gives NaN outside the frame support and propagates DLC NaNs, matching MATLAB interp1 semantics.

7-c.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?
7-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same rule as the expert and the spec: one threshold per session, the 50th percentile of the velocity over the session's (kept-trial) visible bins; below -> 0, at/above -> 1, untracked -> 2. The expert uses np.nanpercentile over the binned array and the AI uses np.median over the visible finite values of kept trials, which are the same quantity. Both produce an almost exactly 50/50 split of the visible bins (AI 3.93%/3.93%).
7-c.code_correctness_justification: median_of restricts to values[keep][visible[keep]] and drops NaNs; discretize initialises everything to 2 and only overwrites where visible & finite, using '>=' for class 1 as the spec requires. The +inf fallback for an empty session is never triggered in this dataset.

7-d.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?
7-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same alignment as the expert: a per-session video-clock offset computed once as mode(sglx.bitcode.bitstart)/sglx.fs - mode(bp.ev.bitStart) (a port of findVideoOffset.m), then frameTimes - offset - goCue[trial], then onto the shared analysis grid. The AI verified the result (video starts at -2.47 s from the go cue, just inside the window) and that tongue visibility jumps right after t=0. The only difference is resampling method: interpolation at bin centres rather than averaging the frames within each bin (see 7-b).
7-d.code_correctness_justification: video_shift is computed once per session and passed into load_video_traces; each view's own frameTimes are used, so the two cameras are handled independently; trials whose corrected frame span does not overlap [TMIN, TMAX] are flagged has_video=False.

8-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Paw velocity* derived from?
8-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses both bottom-camera paw features (top_paw and bottom_paw); the expert uses top_paw alone, arguing that bottom_paw drops out through the delay epoch. The AI's choice is backed by its own per-session measurement (trajectory step 68), which shows that which paw is reliable varies by session -- top_paw is 83% NaN in JEB13_2022-09-21 while bottom_paw is 5%, and the reverse holds in the JEB15 sessions -- and that both are simultaneously missing on only a small fraction of frames. Using whichever paw is tracked therefore gives markedly better coverage (4.4% 'not visible' vs the expert's 18.6%), at the cost of mixing two different forepaws into one speed measure, which makes the variable a movement-magnitude proxy rather than one limb's kinematics. Equally well justified, with a different trade-off.
8-a.code_correctness_justification: PAW_FEATURES lists both (1,'top_paw') and (1,'bottom_paw'); both are read, speeds computed separately, and combined only afterwards.

8-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Paw velocity*?
8-b.decision_correctness_justification: The AI follows the authors' non-tongue path in findPosition.m/findVelocity.m -- nearest-fill the interpolated positions, gradient, subtract the per-trial median frame-to-frame drift, take the magnitude -- and then averages the two paws over whichever was detected, with visibility taken before filling so filled bins are still class 2. The expert computes the same kind of speed at frame resolution with a 5 ms gaussian and no fill or drift subtraction. Both are defensible; the AI's extra steps come straight from the reference code (and it improves on one MATLAB quirk by subtracting each axis's own median drift rather than the x-drift from both). As with the tongue, computing the derivative on the 100 Hz interpolated grid rather than the 400 Hz frames loses some high-frequency content.
8-b.code_correctness_justification: fill=True branch fills x and y, guards the all-NaN case, and returns the pre-fill visibility mask; paw_vis = any over the two paws and paw_speed = nanmean of the visibility-masked speeds, so a bin uses one paw when only one is tracked and is NaN only when neither is -- exactly as described. fill_nearest was verified to implement nearest-value filling in O(n).

8-c.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* thresholded into categories?
8-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same per-session 50th-percentile rule with a third class for untracked bins, identical to the expert and the spec, and applied over kept trials only.
8-c.code_correctness_justification: Same median_of/discretize pair as the tongue, applied to the combined paw speed and paw_vis; observed fractions 0.478/0.478/0.044 show the exact median split of the visible bins.

8-d.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* aligned with the neural data?
8-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same session offset, same per-view frame times, same grid as the tongue and the neural data -- which is also what the expert does. Because the AI reads each view's frameTimes separately, the paw is timed by the bottom camera even where the two cameras recorded different frame counts.
8-d.code_correctness_justification: The trial loop in load_video_traces iterates over view_data, dereferencing that view's own ft_refs[trial] and computing t_rel independently per view before interpolating onto TAXIS.

9-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Motion energy* derived from?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source as the expert: the standalone motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat file (not obj.me, which exists only in some sessions), one trace per trial with one value per side-camera frame, with the nested-struct wrapper unwrapped. The AI probed the on-disk layouts before writing the reader.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: load_motion_energy reads md['me'][0,0]['data'] and unwraps one further level when the result is not an object array, which covers the singly- and doubly-wrapped layouts present in Ephys_Behavior; the conversion ran over all 25 sessions without a motion-energy failure.

9-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Motion energy*?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: Both solutions agree that the value is already one number per frame and needs only resampling. The AI ports loadMotionEnergy.m literally: interp1 onto the analysis axis followed by fillmissing(...,'nearest'), which is exactly what the authors do. The expert instead bin-averages and leaves bins with no frame as NaN. The AI's fidelity to the reference code is a point in its favour, but the nearest-fill extrapolates past the ends of the video support, so almost every bin of every video-covered trial gets a value and the 'no video' class collapses to 0.013% of bins (vs the expert's 3.8%). That effectively removes the third class for this output, which a human might want to check -- but it is the authors' own documented behaviour ('fill nans with nearest value (there are some nans at the start of each trial)'), so it is well justified rather than concerning.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: me[trial] = fill_nearest(interp_nan(TAXIS, t_rel, y)) implements exactly interp1-then-fillmissing; trials with no video or a frame-count mismatch are left all-NaN and me_vis is False for them.

9-c.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* thresholded into categories?
9-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same per-session 50th-percentile split as the expert and the spec, with the third class reserved for trials without usable video. Both solutions deliberately ignore the me.moveThresh shipped with the files, since the spec prescribes a median split. Observed fractions 0.500/0.500/0.0001.
9-c.code_correctness_justification: thr_me = median_of(me, me_vis) and me_cls = discretize(me, me_vis, thr_me) reuse the same helpers; output_values[5] = ['below_median','above_median','no_video'] matches the codes.

9-d.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* aligned with the neural data?
9-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: motion energy has one value per side-camera frame, so it is timed by the side camera's corrected frame times (frameTimes - offset - goCue) and placed on the shared grid. The AI caches those frame times during the video pass and reuses them, and guards against a length mismatch between the motion-energy trace and the side camera's frames.
9-d.code_correctness_justification: frame_times[trial] is populated only for view 0, which is the side camera, and load_motion_energy uses it directly; the y.size != t_rel.size guard prevents silently misaligning a mismatched trace.

10.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
10.decision_correctness_justification: The same philosophy and essentially the same cases as the expert: keep the trial, mark the gap, never interpolate across genuinely missing video. Missing or all-NaN frameTimes, video that does not overlap the window, DLC non-detections, and motion-energy length mismatches all resolve to the 'not visible' class rather than to a dropped trial or a fabricated value; non-string cluster quality labels degrade to '' and the unit is kept; each camera view is timed by its own frame times so mismatched frame counts are handled. The AI audits the outcome (n_trials_without_video = 1 across the dataset). The one substantive difference from the expert is that nearest-filling is applied to paw positions and to motion energy, as the authors' MATLAB does -- but visibility for the paws is recorded before filling, so only motion energy actually gains extrapolated values (see 9-b).
10.code_correctness_justification: Each described guard exists in the code: the frameTimes emptiness/NaN check, the window-overlap check, the all-NaN check in speed_from_position, the y.size != t_rel.size check, _char's non-char fallback, the empty-rates fallback in load_spikes, and the explicit RuntimeWarning suppression around the all-NaN nanmean.

11-a.question: What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?
11-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same conclusion as the expert: file reading dominates. A profile of one two-probe session (2.53 s) attributes ~1.33 s to h5py read_direct -- 1.31 s cumulative in load_video_traces (frameTimes and ts dereferenced once per trial per view) and 0.96 s in load_spikes -- with the only significant compute being my_smooth at 0.54 s. The whole 25-session conversion takes 53 s. The AI did not profile, but its scale judgement (measure wall clock, accept 53 s) is reasonable and its conclusion is the same one the expert reached.
11-a.code_correctness_justification: The profile confirms the description: the HDF5 dereference loops in load_spikes and load_video_traces are the top cumulative entries, and no other stage is comparable.

11-b.question: What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?
11-b.decision_correctness_justification: The AI leaves more vectorisable work in place than the expert, but with no correctness consequence and a lower total runtime (53 s for 25 sessions at 500 bins vs the expert's ~135 s for 44 at 1000). Three loops are genuinely avoidable: the per-trial np.convolve inside my_smooth (0.39 s of 2.53 s per session, replaceable by a single convolve1d along the time axis); the per-cluster spike-binning loop with np.add.at (the expert does the whole probe in one histogram2d, and np.bincount on a flat index would be faster than unbuffered add.at); and the three separate per-trial passes over the video, which could be fused. The per-trial video loops themselves are hard to vectorise for the same reason the expert gives -- each trial has a different number of frames. The AI did partially vectorise (spikes binned across all trials at once) and explicitly rewrote fill_nearest from an O(n^2) nearest-index search to an O(n) two-pass accumulate, so efficiency was on its radar.
11-b.code_correctness_justification: The loops described are present as described, and the profile figures (45,156 np.convolve calls for one session; np.add.at inside the per-cluster loop) confirm the cost attribution.

11-c.question: What processing does the code repeat multiple times?
11-c.decision_correctness_justification: Slightly more repetition than the expert, all of it cheap. The important session-wide quantities are correctly hoisted -- the video offset is computed once per session, the featNames/frameTimes/ts reference lists once per view, the bin grid once at module level -- matching the expert. What is recomputed: the gausswin(15) kernel is rebuilt on every my_smooth call (~1,000 per session), np.diff/np.nanmedian are recomputed per trial and per feature inside speed_from_position, _mode sorts its input twice in video_shift, and the per-trial video loop is traversed three times (positions, then speeds, then motion energy) rather than once. None of it is measurable against the HDF5 read time.
11-c.code_correctness_justification: Each item is verifiable in the source: kern is constructed inside my_smooth; the hoisted view_data/vidshift are constructed once per session; the three per-trial passes are separate loops in load_video_traces, process_session and load_motion_energy.

11-d.question: What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?
11-d.decision_correctness_justification: The expert's answer is 'only in the reading'; the AI does somewhat more discarded work, though none of it affects the output. Kinematics and motion energy are computed for all Ntrials and then indexed by `keep`, so ~10% of that work (834 early-lick/photostim trials) is thrown away -- whereas the neural path correctly bins only the kept trials. Firing rates are smoothed for every quality-passing cluster before the 1 Hz criterion removes most of them. Interpolated x/y positions for three features are materialised as full (n_trials, 500) arrays and discarded once speeds are taken. bp.no is loaded and never used, and the quality bookkeeping (nsingle_units, quality_counts) exists only for session_info. All of this is ordinary slack rather than a design flaw, and the AI did prune one instance of it (removing the unused sample/delay event fields) before finishing.
11-d.code_correctness_justification: The trial loops in load_video_traces, the paw/tongue speed loops and load_motion_energy all iterate over range(n) while only `keep` is written out; my_smooth is called before the mean_fr filter; beh['no'] has no downstream reader.
